    Chapter 1

    What Is Cryptography?

    🤔 Your card number crosses café Wi-Fi, routers and a dozen strangers’ computers. So why can’t any of them read it?

    • ⏱️ ~5 min
    • 📚 8 sections
    • 🎮 3 interactive
    • ⭐ 215 XP
    • 🔑 1 fragment

    1.1A story to start: paying at a café#

    You're at a café, connected to the free Wi-Fi, and you buy a pair of shoes online. You type your card number and tap Pay.

    Think about what that means. Your card number leaves your phone as radio waves. Anyone in the café with a laptop can capture those waves. The café's router, the internet provider, and a dozen other computers between you and the shop all handle your data on the way.

    Yet your card number stays safe. In the fraction of a second before you tapped Pay, your phone:

    1. Checked the shop's ID, to make sure it was really talking to the shop and not an impostor (certificates, Chapter 13).
    2. Agreed on a secret key with the shop, out loud, in front of everyone, without anyone else learning the key (key exchange, Chapter 10).
    3. Scrambled everything it sent using that key, so eavesdroppers see only gibberish (encryption, Chapter 5).
    4. Sealed every piece so that any tampering would be detected (MACs and authenticated encryption, Chapters 5 and 7).

    All four steps are cryptography. This guide explains each one, then shows how they fit together.

    ✔ section read

    1.2The definition#

    Cryptography is the science of protecting information from people who shouldn't see it or change it, even when those people can watch everything you send.

    The word comes from Greek: kryptós ("hidden") + graphein ("to write"). So: "hidden writing."

    Related words you'll hear:

    Word Meaning
    Cryptography Designing ways to protect information
    Cryptanalysis Breaking those protections (the attacker's science)
    Cryptology The whole field: both of the above
    Crypto Short for cryptography. (These days it also means cryptocurrency, which uses cryptography. See Chapter 16.)
    ✔ section read

    1.3What cryptography protects: the five goals#

    Security people usually describe cryptography's job with a handful of goals. Each one answers a simple question:

    Goal The question it answers Everyday analogy Main crypto tools
    Confidentiality Can anyone else read this? A sealed, opaque envelope Encryption
    Integrity Has this been changed? The tamper-evident seal on a medicine bottle Hashes, MACs, signatures
    Authentication Who am I really talking to? Who sent this? Checking someone's ID card Certificates, signatures, MACs, passwords
    Non-repudiation Can the sender deny sending it later? A signature witnessed by a notary Digital signatures
    Availability Can I reach it when I need it? A shop that's open Mostly not crypto's job (that's firewalls, backups, DDoS protection)

    💡 Key idea: Encryption alone only gives you confidentiality. A message can be perfectly secret and still be modified, replayed or sent by an impostor. Real systems combine several tools to get all the goals at once.

    ✔ section read

    1.4Meet the cast#

    Cryptographers explain things with a standard cast of characters. You'll see them throughout this guide:

    Character Role
    Alice Wants to send a secret message
    Bob Wants to receive it
    Eve The eavesdropper. She can listen to everything but can't change anything. (Passive attacker.)
    Mallory The malicious attacker. She can listen, block, modify, replay and inject messages, and pretend to be Alice or Bob. (Active attacker.)
    Trent A trusted third party that both Alice and Bob trust, like a notary or a certificate authority

    On the internet you should always assume Mallory is on the line. Café Wi-Fi, a compromised router, a malicious app, a rogue employee at an internet provider: any of them could be Mallory.

    1.5Basic vocabulary#

    Term Plain meaning Example
    Plaintext The original, readable message MEET ME AT NOON
    Ciphertext The scrambled, unreadable version PHHW PH DW QRRQ
    Cipher (or algorithm) The recipe for scrambling and unscrambling AES, ChaCha20, Caesar cipher
    Key The secret setting that makes the recipe unique to you A 256-bit random number
    Encrypt Plaintext + key → ciphertext
    Decrypt Ciphertext + key → plaintext
    Key space The total number of possible keys Caesar: 25. AES-256: about 10⁷⁷
    ✔ section read

    1.6Encoding vs. encryption vs. hashing (a very common mix-up)#

    These three are often confused, even by professionals. They are completely different things:

    Encoding Encryption Hashing
    Purpose Change the format so data travels safely Keep data secret Create a fingerprint of data
    Uses a key? No Yes No (keyed variants are called MACs)
    Reversible? Yes, by anyone Yes, only with the key No, it's one-way
    Example Base64, hex, URL encoding AES, ChaCha20, RSA SHA-256, SHA-3
    Analogy Translating English to Morse code Locking a letter in a safe Taking a fingerprint

    Example: the text Hello, World! in Base64 is SGVsbG8sIFdvcmxkIQ==. It looks scrambled, but anyone can decode it instantly. It provides zero security.

    ⚠️ Watch out: If someone says a password is "encrypted with Base64," the password is not protected at all. Base64 is a format, like writing in capital letters.

    1.7Kerckhoffs's principle: the lock design is public, the key is secret#

    In 1883, Auguste Kerckhoffs wrote down a rule that still guides every modern system:

    A cryptosystem should be secure even if everything about it, except the key, is public.

    Think of a high-quality door lock. Anyone can buy the same model, take it apart and study it. It's still secure, because your key is unique. Compare that with hiding your house key under the doormat: that's "security through obscurity." It works only until someone finds out the trick.

    That's why the best algorithms (AES, SHA-256, RSA, Ed25519) are completely public, studied by thousands of experts for years. Secret, home-made algorithms usually turn out to be weak once someone looks closely.

    💡 Key idea: In modern cryptography, everything is public except the key. If your security depends on attackers not knowing how your system works, it is not secure.
